transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-16 14:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE); Priya Sharma (Redwood SE); Eliot Park (Head of Platform, Ironbridge); Maya Chen (Engineering Lead); Lucas Rivera (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-section may be imperfect):
- Goal: Understand Ironbridge's cost constraints and tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated vs private; scope a pilot and bench plan.
- Key concerns: monthly token budget, latency SLO for 95th percentile <= 300ms for short prompts, data residency and KMS integration for private deployments, billing visibility.
- Next steps: pricing spreadsheet, benchmark run, security deep-dive.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Moreno: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick round of intros, I'm Alex, AE on the infra team. Priya from engineering will lead the tech bits.
[00:07] Eliot Park: Eliot here, Head of Platform at Ironbridge. Maya and Lucas are with me.
[00:11] Maya Chen: hi.
[00:12] Lucas Rivera: hi all.
[00:13] Priya Sharma: hey folks. excited to dig in.
[00:18] Alex Moreno: high level for today, we want to map your usage patterns, constraints, and then look at per-token levers — batching, prefix caching, quantization options — and how each hosting mode affects unit cost and latency. does that align?
[00:30] Eliot Park: yes. main thing: budget ceiling. we have a hard constraint — about $60k monthly for inference initially. also we need strong auditability for compliance.
[00:38] Alex Moreno: perfect. can you walk through the workloads — burstiness, avg request size, and SLOs?
[00:45] Maya Chen: sure. most requests are short, 80 to 250 tokens. 70% are <128 tokens, about 20% are multi-turn chat with KV cache hits, and we have some nightly batch re-ranking jobs that are long sequences, like 1k tokens but that's 1% of volume. burst pattern: marketing campaigns can triple QPS for 10-30 minute windows.
[01:10] Lucas Rivera: latency targets: product wants 95th <= 300ms for front-end completion on short prompts. longer jobs can be relaxed.
[01:18] Priya Sharma: okay, so short prompts with tight 95th is typical candidate for hosted low-latency instances or dedicated if you need guaranteed throughput. caching of prefixes and persistent KV cache will reduce repeated token compute if you have repeated contexts. are you currently doing any local caching?
[01:35] Maya Chen: we do some naive app-side caching but it's very coarse, TTL-based. no KV level for model serving.
[01:40] Eliot Park: and we prefer not to keep long-lived user data on your side, so we need encryption at rest and KMS integration if private. can you support customer-managed keys?
[01:49] Alex Moreno: yes, both Redwood Private and Dedicated modes support CMK/KMS. hosted can be used with additional protections and SOC2 controls but customer-managed KMS is only in Private today. note: our hosted plan does encryption and SOC2, but CMK is an enterprise add-on.
[02:05] Maya Chen: what's the per-token differential between hosted and dedicated roughly? we saw some back-of-envelope numbers in your docs but wanted a real sense.
[02:12] Alex Moreno: short answer: hosted is higher unit price but zero infra ops and flexible bursting. dedicated has lower per-token compute cost but you pay for reserved capacity and commit. for example, for a 13B-like model hosted might be x, dedicated ~0.7x depending on batch config and quantization. that's fuzzy — we'll send the spreadsheet with modeled rows.
[02:35] Eliot Park: can you unpack batching and cache numbers? if we push batching aggressively, does that hurt our 95th latency?
[02:43] Priya Sharma: yes — batching increases throughput efficiency but adds queuing latency. Redwood's runtime does adaptive batching, so we set a max latency SLO and the runtime will batch as much as it can within that window. for your 95th 300ms target, we typically configure max queue wait <= 40ms and max batch size tuned to the model and GPU. that gives you most of the batching efficiency without increasing tail latency substantially.
[03:05] Lucas Rivera: what's the KV cache hit rate impact?
[03:07] Priya Sharma: if you have good locality — for example repeated system prompts, or same few-turn dialogues — KV cache hits can reduce token compute on the hot path by 30-60% depending on prompt overlap. we can also do prefix caching for static instruction templates.
[03:19] Maya Chen: sounds promising. our main worry is billing surprises. we need line-item visibility - per-call token breakdown - and alerts if burn approaches thresholds.
[03:28] Alex Moreno: we've got token-level reporting, per-route breakdowns, and we can configure usage alerts. in Dedicated you also get capacity telemetry and reserved instance utilization numbers. hosted gives detailed usage logs via our console and API.
[03:40] Eliot Park: ok. on residency — we need EU data residency for some lines of business. can you pin region or do you typically route to nearest available?
[03:48] Alex Moreno: you can pin to region on both Dedicated and Private. hosted is region-aware but falls back for capacity; however we can set routing policies to avoid cross-region fallback for specific customers.
[03:58] Maya Chen: what about fallback policies? if we overload hosted, does it fail open to a smaller model or queue?
[04:04] Priya Sharma: we have automated fallback to compatible model variants and capacity tiers; you can configure canary and A/B fallbacks. for strict latency SLOs you'd likely want Dedicated or Private with burst capacity enabled. hosted can burst but it's subject to capacity availability.
[04:19] Lucas Rivera: let's run some numbers live. assume 1M requests per month, average 120 tokens per request. what's our rough monthly compute cost hosted vs dedicated?
[04:29] Alex Moreno: quick calc: 1M * 120 = 120M tokens. hosted per-token compute rate depends on model. ballpark hosted compute + infra might be $0.000008 per token for a mid-size model — that'd be about $960 monthly compute. but remember there are other line items — network, embedding units, and minimums. dedicated with an effective 30% lower compute rate and amortized infra might be around $672 plus reserved capacity cost. again this is very model/quantization/batching-dependent.
[04:58] Maya Chen: that hosted number seems low relative to our expectations — maybe we're confusing char vs token. also we have embedding usage and some long sequences. can you show a worked example in the spreadsheet?
[05:07] Alex Moreno: yes, we will prepare a worked example. we'll include sample lines for short prompt path, KV cache hit rates at 0%, 30%, 60%, and the impact of batching with queue wait windows.
[05:18] Eliot Park: how do you model the impact of quantization and kernel selection? we plan to run quantized weights to save cost but need to understand accuracy regressions.
[05:26] Priya Sharma: our Optimize toolkit profiles models and suggests quantization levels by workload. 4-bit QAT/LLM quantization often reduces compute cost 2x-4x but you have to validate on your eval set. we tie quality monitoring back to prompt sets and will alert on regressions. for the benchmark we'll run your eval prompts at different quant levels and compare.
[05:44] Maya Chen: great. latency implications of quantization?
[05:47] Priya Sharma: quantized kernels are generally faster per-token on GPU and sometimes faster even on CPU paths, but depends on memory bandwidth and kernel availability. we'll include per-token latency in the benchmark matrix.
[05:58] Lucas Rivera: can we do a hybrid — hosted for low volume and private for higher throughput later?
[06:02] Alex Moreno: absolutely — many customers start hosted to experiment then move to Dedicated or Private when they hit throughput/SLAs or compliance needs. we support consistent API and rollout policies so you don't rewrite client logic.
[06:17] Eliot Park: question on billing for KV cache hits — do you charge for returned tokens on cache hits or only for compute that generates them?
[06:25] Alex Moreno: good question. we bill for requested output tokens and the compute used to generate non-cached tokens. cached KV reuse reduces compute, and in many cases cached tokens are not billed as new generated tokens depending on the integration. we'll detail the billing semantics in the pricing sheet because this is often subtle.
[06:41] Maya Chen: that detail is crucial. can you support sampling and offline re-ranking to shift expensive work to off-peak?
[06:47] Priya Sharma: yes, batch re-ranking during off-peak is a common cost optimization. Redwood supports scheduled batch jobs and you can route those to cheaper capacity pools with different quantization.
[06:58] Lucas Rivera: one more: we have to satisfy audit teams — SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and data purge on deletion. private is easiest for that, but what about hosted?
[07:08] Alex Moreno: hosted offers SSO/SAML and RBAC, and audit logs. data purge and retention policies are configurable; for strict regulatorily requirements customer-managed Private (on VPC) with KMS is the recommended path. we'll surface our SOC2/ISO docs and a data flow diagram.
[07:22] Eliot Park: ok. walk me through a pilot scope that would show us per-token savings and no-regression in quality within 3 weeks.
[07:29] Priya Sharma: proposed pilot: 2-week small-scale benchmark with your representative prompt set (we need the CSV), run on hosted baseline and on a Dedicated reservation-sized instance with same model and quant levels. measure per-call and per-token latency, cache hit improvements, and quality metrics. include a 1-week soak with realistic burst windows to observe autoscaling and fallback behavior. total timeline ~3 weeks including setup.
[07:52] Maya Chen: what minimal commit is needed for Dedicated pilot?
[07:55] Alex Moreno: for a dedicated pilot we can do a 1-month reserved capacity trial with a small commit and provide credits to offset setup. we'll outline options in the pricing doc.
[08:05] Lucas Rivera: we'd like to see a modeled budget that keeps us under $60k/mo. can you present a few scenarios?
[08:12] Alex Moreno: yes — we'll create three scenarios: conservative (no quant, no cache), optimized (30-50% cache hit, moderate batching, 4-bit quant on batch jobs), and aggressive (heavy cache, aggressive batching on non-interactive workloads). each shows expected monthly burn.
[08:28] Eliot Park: what about burst capacity billing? if we need to spike above reserved capacity, how are overages billed?
[08:36] Alex Moreno: overages can be billed at an overage rate; there's also a burst pool option that absorbs short spikes with a blended rate. we'll show blended amortized numbers in the spreadsheet for clarity.
[08:47] Maya Chen: are there minimums or startup fees for Private?
[08:50] Alex Moreno: Private has a platform fee and minimum engagement because of the integration work — network setup, KMS, audit onboarding. we'll include estimates.
[08:59] Lucas Rivera: security deep-dive — what's the typical agenda and who from your side?
[09:03] Priya Sharma: SE + our security engineer attend. agenda: architecture diagram, data flows, encryption, key management, SSO/RBAC, incident response, pen test history, compliance artifacts. estimate 60-90 minutes.
[09:15] Eliot Park: good. we will invite our security and legal leads.
[09:18] Alex Moreno: quick note — you mentioned re-ranking jobs at night. if you can shift those to Dedicated or scheduled cheap pools with aggressive quantization, you can save quite a bit. we'll quantify that.
[09:29] Maya Chen: one practical ask: in the benchmark can you simulate our exact burst traffic?
[09:33] Priya Sharma: yes — if you give us 1 week of traces we can replay at scale. we prefer realistic traces over synthetic patterns.
[09:39] Lucas Rivera: what about network egress costs if we do Private on cloud vs on-prem?
[09:44] Alex Moreno: egress is dependent on hosting location. Private in your VPC will have standard cloud egress; on-prem removes cloud egress but adds ops. we'll include egress estimates in the spreadsheet and highlight which numbers are variable by region.
[09:58] Eliot Park: talk to me about quality monitoring — you mentioned regression alerts tied to prompt sets. how’s that set up?
[10:04] Priya Sharma: we hook into an eval harness: you provide canonical prompt sets and expected outputs or metrics. we run periodic sampling and compare embedding similarity/ROUGE/latency and surface sudden regressions. alerts trigger when metrics cross thresholds.
[10:17] Maya Chen: this is important because if quantization causes hallucination rates to increase we need to rollback automatically.
[10:22] Priya Sharma: we support automatic rollback policies to a safe model variant if quality drops. you can define thresholds per-route.
[10:29] Alex Moreno: we're approaching the meat of next steps. we'll send the pricing workbook, benchmark runbook, and SOC2 pack. timeline: Alex sends pricing by Friday, Priya sets up benchmark slots next week, we do the 2-week pilot, then security deep-dive while pilot runs.
[10:45] Eliot Park: sounds good. couple of smaller points: 1) can we get per-route throttles to protect paid services? 2) do you support per-team billing buckets?
[10:55] Alex Moreno: yes to both — per-route throttles and token quotas are supported and we have billing buckets and cost centers in the console.
[11:02] Maya Chen: ok. any rough risks we should call out?
[11:05] Priya Sharma: risks: quality regressions from quant; tail latency from over-batching; cross-region fallbacks that violate residency if misconfigured. mitigation: benchmark, per-route routing policies, and regression monitoring.
[11:17] Lucas Rivera: good. what level of instrumentation do you need from our side to run replay tests?
[11:22] Priya Sharma: ideally a CSV with timestamp, prompt, expected avg tokens, and a few metadata fields; also a target time-window for the burst pattern. we can take care of load generation.
[11:33] Eliot Park: we'll pull that together.
[11:35] Alex Moreno: anything else from you?
[11:37] Maya Chen: please be explicit about billing semantics for cached tokens and re-renders. that's the one that will need legal sign-off.
[11:44] Alex Moreno: acknowledged — we'll add a billing explainer section in the sheet.
[11:48] Lucas Rivera: one last thing — do you have case studies for similar fintech customers with strict residency and tight budgets?
[11:54] Alex Moreno: yes, we have a couple — we'll add anonymized references and a short case summary.
[12:01] Eliot Park: perfect. thanks, everyone.
[12:03] Priya Sharma: thanks, we'll follow up quickly.
[12:06] Alex Moreno: meeting wrap-up: recap of next steps and owners. thanks all.

End of transcript
